summary:
Charts of Earth data show lines going up or down, but never say whether the change is real or just chance. Weather is noisy, so random ups and downs often look like trends: on simulated data with no trend, textbook tests call about 1 series in 4 "significant".

Chance or Change is a free website that turns students into trend detectives. They open a "case": pick a measurement (heat, water, air, sunlight or soil), a place and the years. It builds the time series from 45 years of NASA data, and two statistical tests must agree before a trend counts. Each case gets a plain-English verdict and a stamp: CASE CLOSED, CASE OPEN (with the years of data still needed) or NO TREND FOUND.

Three features make it a detective game:
- The evidence timeline shows when a trend became proven: Svalbard's warming (+0.67 °C per decade) was proven in 2004.
- "Real or fake?": spot the real NASA record among three fakes with the same noise.
- A world map of 576 places shows where a measurement rises and where it falls.

Why it matters: students learn to ask "could this be chance?" before believing a chart.
details:
What it does

Chance or Change is a free website (it also works on a phone) where a student opens a "case" in four steps: what to investigate, where, which years and which measurement. The case file shows:

  • the monthly values and the anomalies (each month compared with its normal), with the trend line and its 95% band;
  • a stamp (CASE CLOSED, CASE OPEN or NO TREND FOUND), the rate of change per decade and a verdict in plain English;
  • the evidence timeline: the year the trend became proven;
  • every statistic behind the verdict, a downloadable case file and a share link.

Seven tabs: Investigate (open any case), Line-up (every measurement for a region, ranked by the strength of the evidence), World map (576 places, with a "see-saw finder" for places moving in opposite directions), Real or fake? (the game), Demo cases (two guided cases: the Arctic's warming and the Sahel's rain), Method check and Glossary.

How it works

  1. Data. The website downloads monthly values from NASA POWER for a region (a box about 4° across) and averages every model grid tile inside it. For the Sahel and Los Angeles it also reads satellite time series made with NASA Giovanni.
  2. Removing the seasons. Each calendar month's normal is removed, so the seasons (far bigger than any trend) don't hide it.
  3. Two tests that must agree. A straight trend line (adjusted for autocorrelation) and the Mann-Kendall test with the Hamed-Rao correction. The headline p-value is the larger of the two, so a trend counts only when both tests agree.
  4. Honest about many tests. The world map (576 places) and the line-up (all measurements of a region) apply the Benjamini-Hochberg correction.
  5. Case files. The stamp uses the headline p-value and the years of data needed to detect a trend of this size (Weatherhead et al., 1998). The evidence timeline re-runs the test using only the data up to each year, so no later data leak in.
  6. Fair fakes. The game's fakes copy the real record's noise, its month-to-month memory and each calendar month's own spread, so they can't be spotted for the wrong reason.

Benefits and intended impact

  • For students (high school and university): an honest answer to "is this change real?" for any place on Earth, in plain words, in under a minute, with no sign-up and nothing to install.
  • For teachers: two guided cases and a game that move a lesson from "look at this chart" to "how do we know?", plus a glossary of every term.
  • The intended impact: people who ask "could this be chance?" before they believe, or dismiss, a chart about our planet.

How it is creative

  • The evidence timeline answers a question most charts never ask: not only "is the trend real?" but "since when has it been proven?".
  • "Real or fake?" turns a statistics idea (surrogate data) into a game, then shows how often a fake fools the simple test but not the honest one.
  • Case stamps. CASE OPEN says about how many more years of data would settle the case, so "we don't know yet" becomes something a student can understand.
  • Two witnesses. For the Sahel, the weather model and the satellites are put side by side, and the gap between them is tested too.
  • The see-saw finder shows the same measurement rising in one place and falling in another: "same planet, opposite directions".

Factors considered

Honesty before excitement. A verdict needs two tests to agree; trends found among many tests are corrected for it; and the app says CASE OPEN when the data can't settle a case yet.

Checking the method.

  • False alarms. On 2,000 simulated series with no trend but with autocorrelation like real weather, the plain tests called a trend in about 24% of them. The app's headline test did so in 4.8%, close to the 5% it promises. The Method check tab re-runs a smaller version live.
  • A known trend is found. On simulated data with a trend of 0.3 per decade, the app finds 0.3 ± 0.1.
  • A published measurement. Nordli et al. (2020) report that the weather station at Svalbard Airport warmed by 1.7 °C per decade from 1991 to 2018. For the same years, the app finds +1.04 for the Svalbard region and +1.17 for the model tile at the station: the same direction, and somewhat smaller, as expected for a model average compared with one coastal station.
  • Two witnesses. In the Sahel, the model's rainfall and the GPM satellites agree month by month (correlation 0.975), but since 2001 the model's rise is about three times the satellite's. A test of their difference shows the gap is real (p = 0.017), so the app tells students to trust the direction more than the size.
  • 90 automatic tests check the statistics, the data and the website.

Reliability. Backup copies of all ten preset regions are built in, so the demo cases work even if NASA's servers are down.

Plain language. Every verdict is a sentence a student can read, with the official statistical terms explained in the glossary.

Limits, stated in the app.

  • Values are averages over model grid tiles, not readings from one weather station.
  • Over Antarctica the model has few observations to keep it on track, so the app marks those points "treat with care".
  • A significant trend shows that something changed, not why.

What the data show (examples)

  • Svalbard (Arctic Norway): air temperature rose by 0.67 °C per decade from 1981 to 2025, very unlikely to be chance (p = 5.7e-09), proven in 2004.
  • The world: at 71% of 576 grid points the air temperature trend is very unlikely to be chance, and 373 of those 408 points are warming. The fastest is the Arctic: +1.23 °C per decade at 80°N, 70°E.
  • Los Angeles: nitrogen dioxide from traffic and industry, measured from space, more than halved from 2005 to 2025 (proven in 2015).
  • The Sahel: probably getting wetter since 2001, but by less than the model says, and not yet proven by the satellites (about 12 more years of data needed).

How NASA data make it possible

Trend tests need long, regular and consistent records. NASA POWER gives monthly values from 1981 for any place on Earth, made the same way everywhere, so any region and period can be tested fairly: MERRA-2 for temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind and soil wetness, and GEWEX SRB and CERES for sunlight and cloud cover. GPM IMERG rainfall and OMI nitrogen dioxide, made into time series with NASA Giovanni, give an independent check from space. Every dataset is listed with its link under "NASA Data".

Tools and technologies

Python 3.12; Streamlit (the website); pandas and NumPy (data); statsmodels, SciPy and pymannkendall (statistics); Plotly (charts and maps); requests (the NASA POWER API); pytest (90 automatic tests). Hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud. The demo video was recorded from the live website with Playwright and edited with FFmpeg.

Use of AI (SI) tools

Chance or Change was built with Claude Code, Anthropic's AI coding tool. Where and how it was used:

  • Ideas, research and analysis: Claude Code helped plan the project and brainstorm its features and name, find sources (for example the published Svalbard record), and run and summarise the analysis.
  • Code: Claude Code wrote the code and the tests, following a written plan. Every code file starts with a line saying it was written with Claude Code (AI), and the website's footer says so too.
  • Text: the website's wording, the documentation and this page's text were drafted with Claude Code and reviewed by the author.
  • Data: all data are NASA's. The result files inside the app (the world map's trends and the line-ups) were worked out from NASA data by this code.
  • Design: the website's layout and colours and the video's title cards were made with Claude Code. No AI-generated images are used, and no NASA logos or other NASA branding.
  • Video: the demo is a screen recording of the live website, recorded and edited by scripts that Claude Code wrote. It shows a "Made with SI/AI tools" label the whole time, and the same note is in the file's metadata.
  • Audio: the narration is a synthetic voice (macOS text-to-speech) reading a script drafted with Claude Code.

The app itself contains no AI or machine learning: its verdicts come from classical statistical tests.

The author set the goals, made the design and data decisions (for example: both tests must agree; testing the gap between the two witnesses), signed in to NASA's services, deployed the website, and reviewed and tested the results, including on a phone.
